planting.note: Start seed indoors with a cool stratification period, then move young plants into a lean, sharply drained crevice or wall planting once frost danger passes.

directions: This trailing bellflower forms a loose rosette of leathery, toothed leaves from which arching stems droop over rock faces, each tipped with flask-shaped buds that open to white, pink-flushed bells in early summer. It is native to limestone cliffs and ravines of northeastern Turkey and the Caucasus, where its roots wedge into vertical crevices far from standing moisture. In cultivation it performs best planted sideways into a stone wall, raised trough, or steep scree so water drains immediately away from the crown rather than pooling around it. Established plants tolerate considerable summer heat as long as winter wet is kept off the foliage.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (Seed Exchange)

planting.note: Start seed indoors and transplant young rosettes into a gritty, neutral-to-alkaline scree bed or vertical crevice after frost danger passes.

directions: Wanner's bellflower is a diminutive cliff-dweller from the Dinaric mountains of the western Balkans, forming small basal rosettes of hairy, toothed leaves that hug limestone fissures. Short stems carry a handful of upward-facing, deep violet-blue bells in midsummer, held just clear of the foliage mat. It is seldom seen outside specialist rock garden collections and prefers the same vertical, fast-draining crevice culture as its better-known relative Campanula zoysii, resenting any standing winter moisture around the crown. A raised scree bed or tufa planting mimicking its native cliff habitat gives the most reliable results.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (Seed Exchange)

planting.note: Sow seed in fall into pots left outdoors for winter chilling, since germination is erratic without sustained cold; transplant small rosettes into a gritty, acidic scree the following spring.

directions: Lagger's rock jasmine forms a dense, silver-haired cushion of tiny overlapping rosettes that disappears under a flush of relatively large, deep pink flowers with a contrasting eye each spring. It is native to acidic schist and granite screes high in the Pyrenees, where constant snowmelt keeps roots cool while surface drainage stays razor-sharp. Like most high-alpine Androsace, it resents the combination of summer humidity and winter wet far more than cold itself, so a raised scree bed, tufa pocket, or alpine house pot with a lean, gritty mix suits it far better than an ordinary border. Top-dressing the cushion with fine grit helps keep foliage dry and rot-free through wet spells.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (Seed Exchange)

planting.note: Start seed indoors and transplant into a lean, gritty, alkaline scree or trough mix in full sun once seedlings are sturdy.

directions: Freyn's pink builds a tight, blue-gray cushion of needle-fine foliage scattered across limestone outcrops of the central Balkan Peninsula, staying almost flush with the rock it grows from. Solitary pale to deep pink flowers sit directly on the cushion in early summer, barely raised above the foliage, a habit shared by several small Balkan cushion dianthus. It wants the same scrupulous drainage and lean, calcareous grit as alpine saxifrages, and quickly declines if planted in rich or moisture-retentive soil. A trough or raised scree bed where water never lingers around the crown is the most reliable home for it.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (Seed Exchange)

planting.note: Start seed indoors and move young plants into a gritty, lime-rich scree bed or trough once established, siting them where drainage is immediate.

directions: One of the smallest cushion pinks in general cultivation, this high-elevation Balkan species forms a dense, moss-like mat of tiny grey-green leaves barely an inch tall on open limestone ridges. Pale to rose-pink flowers open almost stemless directly on the cushion surface in early summer, giving the whole plant a speckled appearance rather than showing distinct blooms above the foliage. Its minute scale makes it a favorite for troughs and miniature rock gardens, but it demands the sharpest possible drainage and resents any organic mulch touching the crown. Gritty, mineral soil and a cool root zone are essential for keeping it alive through a humid summer.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (Seed Exchange)

planting.note: Start seed indoors and transplant into gritty, well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline soil in a raised bed or scree once frost danger passes.

directions: Named for the fine parallel veining on its narrow leaves, this Balkan and Greek mountain pink spreads into a loose gray-green mat that drapes attractively over rock edges. Bright rose-pink flowers with finely fringed petal margins open just above the foliage in early summer, more generously than many of its tighter cushion-forming relatives. It grows naturally in open, rocky pasture and scree at mid-to-high elevations, so it tolerates slightly richer soil than the smallest cushion dianthus while still needing fast drainage. Give it full sun and a lean, gritty bed, and shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat compact.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (Seed Exchange)

planting.note: Start seed indoors and set young plants into a lean, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun after frost danger passes.

directions: True to its name, this pink from the Pyrenees and nearby French limestone ranges holds its pale to deep pink flowers almost stemless against a tight, blue-green cushion of narrow leaves. It forms dense, hard mounds on open rocky pasture and scree where grazing and poor soil keep taller plants from crowding it out. In the garden it wants exactly that lean, mineral, fast-draining environment, performing poorly wherever fertility or moisture linger around the crown. A scree bed, raised trough, or gravel-topped rock garden pocket reproduces its native conditions most closely.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (Seed Exchange)

planting.note: Sow seed in fall into pots left outdoors for winter chilling, since germination is slow and uneven without extended cold; transplant small rosettes the following spring into gritty, lean soil.

directions: Like most rock garden drabas, this Caucasus and eastern Turkey species forms a tiny, tightly packed cushion of rosetted leaves wedged into limestone crevices, producing a dusting of small four-petaled yellow flowers on short stems in earliest spring. Its scale and habit closely echo the better-known Draba aizoides, but it remains a scarcer choice reserved mostly for specialist alpine collections. It thrives in the leanest possible mineral soil with constant drainage, since any accumulated moisture around the tightly packed rosettes quickly leads to rot. A trough, raised scree bed, or tufa pocket replicates its native cliff-ledge habitat far better than open garden soil.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (Seed Exchange)

planting.note: Surface-sow fresh seed in fall and leave pots exposed to winter cold, since gentian seed needs light plus sustained chilling and is notoriously slow and erratic to germinate.

directions: Paradox gentian takes its name from its unusually narrow, almost grass-like leaves, a striking departure from the broader foliage typical of most cushion gentians, native to subalpine meadows and rocky slopes of the Caucasus. Deep blue, upward-facing trumpet flowers open from late summer into autumn on wiry stems rising just above the thin foliage clumps. It wants steady moisture through the growing season paired with sharp drainage in winter, a balance best achieved in a humus-enriched scree or raised bed with light afternoon shade in hotter climates. Established clumps take a couple of seasons to reach flowering size but are long-lived once settled.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (Seed Exchange)

planting.note: Fall-sow onto lean, gravelly soil and leave exposed to winter cold, since seed needs a full cold-stratification period to break dormancy reliably.

directions: Sticky phlox forms low, wiry mats of narrow, gland-covered foliage that feels tacky to the touch, a trait that likely helps deter browsing on the dry, rocky slopes of the interior Pacific Northwest it calls home. Clusters of pale pink to lavender flowers open along the stems in mid-spring, well suited to a gravel garden or scree bed mimicking the open, sun-baked ground where it grows wild. Like other western native mat phlox, it demands lean, fast-draining soil and resents summer irrigation once established, rotting quickly if kept consistently damp. It is a good companion for other high-desert rock garden natives in a dry, sunny scree planting.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (Seed Exchange)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in a gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained scree mix in partial shade or morning sun, protected from winter wet, using the same alpine-house or raised-bed culture as other pubescens hybrids.

directions: 'Christine' is a long-cultivated garden selection within the Primula x pubescens group, the same auricula-relative hybrid swarm that produced 'Rufus', forming compact rosettes of softly hairy leaves topped by clusters of deep purple-red flowers with a small pale eye in spring. It shares the pubescens hybrids' preference for a gritty, sharply drained scree or raised alpine bed, needing protection from prolonged winter wet far more than from cold itself. Its rich flower color sits toward the darker, more saturated end of the pubescens color range, making it a useful contrast to paler cultivars in a trough or alpine-house collection. Divide congested clumps every few years after flowering to maintain vigor.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (Seed Exchange)

planting.note: Sow seed in fall and leave pots exposed to winter chilling, since dodecatheon seed germinates slowly and unevenly without sustained cold; transplant seedlings the following spring into humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil.

directions: 'Aphrodite' is a named selection of the eastern North American shooting star chosen for its especially rich magenta-pink reflexed flowers, carried in nodding umbels atop leafless stems above a basal rosette of soft, spoon-shaped leaves in mid-spring. Like the species, it goes dormant and disappears entirely by midsummer, so it is best paired with later-emerging companions that can fill the gap it leaves in a woodland rock garden or shaded border. It prefers humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist through spring but tolerates drier conditions once it has died back for the season. Self-sown seedlings may not come true to the deeper color, so division of an established clump is the most reliable way to increase the named form.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (Seed Exchange)
